'''Giovanni Fazio''' (1933 or 1934 – February 12, 2026) was an American physicist at [[Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics|Center for Astrophysics {{!}} Harvard & Smithsonian]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.researchgate.net/scientific-contributions/2026153497_Giovanni_Fazio |title=Giovanni Fazio's research works: Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, Cambridge and other places |website=ResearchGate |language=en |access-date=2020-01-07}}</ref> He was an [[astrophysicist]] who has initiated and participated in multiple [[Space observatories|observation]] programs.

==Career==
In 1962 he joined the [[Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory]] and the [[Harvard College Observatory]]. There he started a program in [[gamma-ray astronomy]] using balloon-borne and ground-based detectors,<ref name="Homepage at Harvard-Smithsonian">{{cite web |title=Giovanni G. Fazio|website=Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics |url=https://www.cfa.harvard.edu/~gfazio/ |accessdate=12 July 2019}}</ref> and the construction of the 10-meter optical reflector at the [[F. L. Whipple Observatory]], Arizona, for the search of ultra-high-energy [[Cosmic ray|cosmic]] [[Gamma ray|gamma-rays]].

In 1984 Fazio was selected as Principal Investigator for the [[Infrared Array Camera]] (IRAC) experiment on the [[Spitzer Space Telescope]] ([[NASA]]). The telescope was launched in August 2003, and has since produced multiple discoveries and images of the infrared universe.

Fazio was the [[editor-in-chief]] of ''[[Journal of Astronomical Instrumentation]]''. He was also the main editor of ''The Encyclopedia of Cosmology''.<ref>{{cite book |editor-last=Fazio |editor-first=Giovanni |title=The Encyclopedia of Cosmology |publisher=World Scientific |isbn=978-981-4656-19-1 |doi=10.1142/9496 |year=2018 |volume=1 }}</ref>

==Death==
Fazio died on February 12, 2026, at the age of 92.<ref>[https://www.eatonfuneralhomes.com/obituary/Giovanni-Fazio Giovannia Fazio]</ref>

==Awards==
In recognition of his scientific contribution, Fazio has received many international awards. He was awarded the 2015 [[Henry Norris Russell Lectureship]] for "his pioneering work on gamma-ray and infrared instrumentation, which has advanced our understanding in many areas of astronomy, ranging from near-Earth objects to high-redshift galaxies."<ref>{{cite web |title=Henry Norris Russell Lectureship |url=https://aas.org/grants-and-prizes/henry-norris-russell-lectureship |website=American Astronomical Society |accessdate=16 January 2020}}</ref>

In 2019, Fazio received the [[SPIE]] George W. Goddard Award in Space and Airborne Optics "in recognition of exceptional achievements in the area of infrared instruments spanning 40 years including the Infrared Array Camera (IRAC) aboard the Spitzer Space Telescope, which has made extraordinary discoveries from measuring the mass of the most distant galaxy (GN-z11) to finding and characterizing seven Earth-sized planets in the TRAPPIST-1 system."<ref name="SPIE Award">{{cite web |title=SPIE George W. Goddard Award in Space and Airborne Optics |url=http://spie.org/about-spie/awards-programs/awards-listing/spie-george-w-goddard-award-in-space-and-airborne-optics?SSO=1 |website=SPIE |accessdate=12 July 2019}}</ref>

He was elected a Legacy Fellow of the [[American Astronomical Society]] in 2020. <ref> {{cite web|url=https://aas.org/grants-and-prizes/aas-fellows|title=AAS Fellows|publisher=AAS|accessdate=27 September 2020}} </ref>
